Detection physics

Between two SPHEREx passes (6 months) Earth moves ~2 AU. A body at distance d shifts by about 2 AU / d against the stars.

13.8′ ≈ 133 SPHEREx pixels (6.2″)

Stars are effectively fixed. Variable stars change brightness, not position. A mover that shifts by this amount and then continues along a smooth track is a candidate.

The five test targets. Each opens a real-image flipbook across survey epochs.

1 · What is SPHEREx?

A NASA telescope launched in March 2025. It photographs the whole sky in 102 infrared colours (0.75–5 µm) and repeats the map every six months. Your eye sees 3 colours; SPHEREx sees 102, and each colour reveals something different: stars, dust, ice. Data Release 1: 12 November 2026.

2 · Pick a colour band

Tap a block. The top row is SPHEREx’s six bands (17 colours each = 102). The other rows are older surveys: tap one to show it on the map.

3 · The first all-sky map

Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom.

4 · How sky images improved

DSS21950s–90s · photographic plates, ~1″ pixels, optical only
2MASS1997–2001 · near-infrared over the whole sky
WISE2010 · 2.75″ pixels, 3.4–22 µm, found brown dwarfs and asteroids
Pan-STARRS2010–14 · 0.25″ pixels, sharp digital optical
SPHEREx2025– · 6.2″ pixels but 102 colours, repeated every six months

Newer is not always sharper: SPHEREx trades pixel sharpness for colour. That is why it can separate ice, dust and stars.

Deep-sky database: NGC/IC/Messier (OpenNGC) cross-matched with the NASA Hubble sky-map list. ★ marks NASA Hubble objects.

Method

1. Pick a target or position. 2. Blink the same patch through surveys from different decades. 3. Objects that jump while the background stays fixed are movers. 4. Compare the shift with the parallax expectation and the proper-motion track. 5. Save coordinates (CSV).

Solar system on the real sky ·

Planet positions are computed from approximate NASA/JPL orbital elements for 2025–2028.

3I/ATLAS is the third known interstellar object. SPHEREx observed it in August 2025 and again in December 2025, with another pass planned for April 2026 (IRSA, SPHEREx team).

On our computed orbit the comet moves about 89° across the sky between the first two visits and about 60° by April.

From the IRSA observation table: 259 spectral images in 133 exposures, 1–15 Aug and 8–14 Dec 2025. Our orbit agrees with the positions predicted by the SPHEREx team to 0.02° (median).
